## What is 'practicum'?

A practicum is a supervised, hands-on course of study.
We intend this book as a practicum in the fullest
sense: it teaches skills that cannot be acquired by
reading, only by doing. Every chapter closes with
exercises that require the reader to sit at a
keyboard and produce an artifact, whether that is a
Git commit, a Docker container, or a finished
analysis report.

The book is the companion to *Statistical Computing
in the Age of AI*, the methods-focused volume. The
two books cover complementary territory. The methods
volume teaches what to compute and why; this volume
teaches how to compute it reproducibly. That is,
where the methods volume is concerned with the
substance of an analysis, the present volume is
concerned with the practice by which that analysis
is made to survive scrutiny.

## What this book covers

We begin with an account of the territory the book
covers, which is the practical work of
biostatistical data analysis. The book is organized
into eight parts, and every chapter belongs to one of
them. @tbl-intro-parts names, for each part, the
question it answers, its chapters, and the tools it
teaches. Parts I to III are the first quarter of the
two-quarter sequence: why the work is done this way,
the tools it is done with, and the path from raw files
to a dataset you can trust. Parts IV to VIII are the
second quarter: the document and environment that make
the analysis rebuildable, the plan and tests that make
it defensible, the industrial conventions it may have
to meet, its delivery to an audience, and a capstone
that does all of it on one study.

| Part | The question it answers | Chapters | Key tools |
|---|---|---|---|
| Why and with whom | Why work reproducibly, and what do you owe your collaborators and the people in the data? | @sec-why, @sec-team-science, @sec-deident | The three kinds of reproducibility, the intake conversation, the HIPAA pathways |
| Your toolkit | What do you work with every day, and how do you keep a history of it? | @sec-shell, @sec-workstation, @sec-git-solo, @sec-git-teams, @sec-ai-coding | The shell, R and an IDE, Git and GitHub, language models and coding agents |
| Data in hand | How do raw files become an analysis dataset you can trust? | @sec-acquisition, @sec-apis, @sec-wrangling, @sec-types, @sec-joins, @sec-databases, @sec-graphics, @sec-missing, @sec-deident-practice | `readr`, `dplyr`, `tidyr`, `forcats`, `stringr`, `lubridate`, SQL and `dbplyr`, `ggplot2`, `naniar`, `mice` |
| Documents and environments | How does the analysis rebuild, as a document, on someone else's machine? | @sec-quarto, @sec-renv, @sec-docker, @sec-zzcollab, @sec-targets, @sec-cloud | Quarto, `renv`, Docker, the research compendium, `targets`, remote compute |
| Analysis practice | How do you show that the analysis was planned in advance and computes what it claims? | @sec-analysis-plan, @sec-testing | The SAP and DMSP, Git tags, `tinytest`, GitHub Actions |
| Industry | How does the work meet the conventions of regulated drug development? | @sec-cdisc, @sec-sas | SDTM, ADaM, SAS |
| Analysis to audience | How does a finished analysis reach its readers honestly, and in a form they can check? | @sec-penguins, @sec-adni, @sec-ethics, @sec-communicating, @sec-federal | Computed reports, the memo, the response to reviewers, repositories and DOIs |
| Capstone | Can you take one study from raw export to deposit? | @sec-synthesis | All of the above |

: The book's eight parts, in the single-volume site's order. A
printed volume may group or order these parts differently for its
own binding; its own table of contents is the authority for what
number a part or chapter carries in your hands. {#tbl-intro-parts}

The order is a dependency order. The first quarter ends
with data in hand because everything in the second
quarter acts on a dataset: a Quarto document reports on
it, a container pins the environment that built it, a
plan constrains what may be done with it, and a deposit
archives it. In this ordering, ethics and deposition come
late, deliberately. Deposition is instruction about
handing over something you have not built until then.
The ethics chapter argues that the entire infrastructural
apparatus of this book is orthogonal to whether an
analysis misleads, and that argument can only land once
the apparatus has been built. (A print volume may place
the ethics chapter earlier, beside de-identification, as a
prerequisite rather than a conclusion; either order
teaches the same argument.)

Eight appendices follow: alternative wrangling
paradigms for reading code that is not tidyverse
(@sec-alternative-wrangling), the peer-program survey
on which several chapters rest their case for existing
(@sec-peer-survey), an inventory of the lab's own
software, which several chapters use and which we
disclose rather than distribute quietly
(@sec-lab-software), a glossary (@sec-glossary), an
instructor guide (@sec-instructor-guide), the
AI-tooling landscape as of this edition (@sec-tooling),
a guide to migrating R Markdown projects
(@sec-rmd-migration), and an index to every chapter's
cheat sheet (@sec-cheat-sheets).

@fig-book-map is the shape of the whole, and it is
worth a moment before starting: the parts are not
independent modules but a dependency chain, and a
reader who skips ahead will find the later parts
assuming the earlier ones.

## What this book does not cover

- The statistical theory underlying specific
  models (linear, generalized linear, mixed,
  survival). For that, see the companion book
  *Statistical Computing in the Age of AI* or a
  standard reference.
- Experimental design, sample-size calculation,
  or causal inference beyond what is needed to
  execute an analysis plan.
- Specialized computing platforms (Bioconductor,
  Stan, deep-learning frameworks) beyond brief
  mention.
- The algorithms of computational statistics:
  numerical optimization, Monte Carlo and simulation
  design, the bootstrap, and Bayesian computation.
  These dominate many peer statistical-computing
  courses; here they are the territory of the
  companion volume, and we treat their absence as
  deliberate rather than accidental.
- Statistical theory in any depth.

The trade-off is deliberate. On the one hand, a
deeper treatment of any single method would merit a
volume of its own. On the other, the analyst who
cannot move a finished analysis through the full
workflow is poorly served by depth alone. We have
therefore aimed for breadth across the workflow
rather than depth on any one method.

## Who this book is for

The intended reader is a graduate student or
early-career biostatistician who has working R
fluency and is now learning to operate
professionally: that is, working on teams,
satisfying regulatory requirements, and producing
reproducible artifacts that survive peer review.

We assume the following of the reader:

- R proficiency at the level of *R for Data
  Science* (Wickham and Grolemund).
- Familiarity with statistical methods at the
  master's level (linear and generalized linear
  models, basic survival, regression diagnostics).
- Comfort with the command line and basic file-
  system operations.

We do not, on the other hand, assume any of the
following:

- Prior Git, Docker, or `renv` experience.
- Prior collaboration with clinical investigators.
- Experience with regulatory or
  industry-sponsored research.

## How to read this book

For each chapter, the workflow we recommend is the
following:

1. **Read** the chapter through once, without
   running code. Notice the structure: the card,
   the opening quiz, the sections with their
   checks and callouts, the exercises.
2. **Replicate** the examples in your own
   environment. Type, do not copy-paste. The
   typing forces you to read each character; the
   copy-paste does not.
3. **Do** the exercises without consulting an
   LLM. The cognitive cost of producing the
   answer yourself is, it appears, part of the
   learning.
4. **Extend** by sending the LLM prompt callouts
   to a language model and critiquing the
   responses against your own work.

The book is, we grant, somewhat dense. Reading two
chapters per week is a sustainable pace, which makes
the whole book a two-quarter sequence, Parts I to
III in the first quarter and Parts IV to VIII in the
second; a one-quarter core path of twenty chapters is
laid out in the preface. We would
emphasize that the exercises are the work. The
chapters are merely the scaffolding.

## The habits this book teaches {#sec-habits}

The book has one idea under all of its tools: **make
silent failures loud.** The errors that damage an
analysis are rarely the ones that stop it. A join
that multiplies rows, a package update that changes a
number, and a figure built from a stale intermediate
file all run without complaint. Each chapter teaches
a habit that turns one of those quiet failures into a
loud one, and each habit below is numbered so that
later chapters can point back to it.

{{< include _habits.md >}}

You do not need to memorize the list now. Every
chapter ends by naming the habits it has exercised,
and @sec-synthesis returns to the whole list.

## Getting help {#sec-getting-help}

Ask in the course forum first, where the people answering know
the book and the running study. Beyond the course, Posit Community
(<https://forum.posit.co>) answers questions about R, the
tidyverse, Quarto, and RStudio, and Stack Overflow answers
well-posed programming questions tagged `r`.

Whoever you ask, send a minimal reproducible example: the smallest
code, with the smallest synthetic data, that shows the problem.
The `reprex` package runs your code in a clean session and formats
the code and its output for pasting, so a missing `library()` call
or an object that exists only in your workspace shows up before
anyone else sees it. A display-only example:

```{.r}
reprex::reprex({
  library(dplyr)
  visits <- tibble::tibble(id = c(1, 1, 2), sbp = c(120, NA, 135))
  visits |>
    summarize(mean_sbp = mean(sbp))
})
```

A reprex is habit 1 at its smallest scale: code and data that
travel together and run on someone else's machine. Building one
often answers the question before you post it.

Never post protected health information, rows of any dataset held
under a data-use agreement, or credentials such as tokens,
passwords, and keys, even in a private message. The rules are the
same as for a language model (habit 12), and @sec-ai-governance
sets them out: send structure, not data.

To report an error in this book, open an issue in the repository's
issue tracker (<https://github.com/rgt47/practicum/issues>); each
page of the HTML edition links to it. Name the chapter and section,
quote the passage, and say what you expected.

## The chapter pattern

Every chapter follows the same template, and the
Conventions page before this introduction describes
its visual elements. In order:

- **Opening.** A paragraph that states the problem
  the chapter solves, usually as a failure that runs
  without error, followed by an epigraph.
- **Pipeline diagram.** The analysis pipeline with
  the stage the chapter teaches highlighted.
- **Chapter card.** Reading time; what you'll need
  from earlier chapters and which packages the code
  loads; what you'll be able to do; and an outline.
- **Skip ahead?** Three open-ended questions, in the
  style of *Advanced R* [@wickham2019advr]. If all
  three come easily, you can bypass the chapter.
  Answers appear in the Prerequisites-answers section
  at the end, and each quiz links directly to them.
- **Sections.** Each teaches one idea through a
  worked example on the running study, and ends with
  exercises (solutions folded beneath them) and a
  **Check**: a short question with its answer folded
  inside.
- **Callouts within the sections.** A
  **Verification** is a command that confirms a
  worked example did what it claims; a **Pitfall** is
  a silent failure that analysts actually hit; an
  **LLM prompt** is a prompt for a language model or
  coding agent, placed beside the task it helps with,
  together with the check that verifies its output.
- **Rules of thumb.** The numbered habits the chapter
  has exercised, each restated as a rule.
- **Cumulative practice.** Exercises that combine
  this chapter with earlier ones, and one to do on
  your own work.
- **Cheat sheet.** The chapter's commands in one
  table, each with the check that confirms it worked.
- **Further reading** and **Prerequisites answers.**

The pattern is repeated deliberately. By the third
chapter, the reader will know where to find each
component.

## On the Age-of-AI framing

The companion textbook is titled *Statistical
Computing in the Age of AI*. This Practicum is named
for its content (Biostatistics Practicum) rather than
the AI framing, but the framing is present throughout.
Chapters carry LLM prompt callouts showing how to use
AI assistance for the chapter's tools, each with the
check that verifies the output, and @sec-ai-coding is
the chapter on AI-assisted coding more generally. The
'LLM' in the callout title is shorthand. It covers
both a chat interface and a coding agent, such as
Claude Code, that reads a project's files and edits
them directly. @sec-ai-coding treats the distinction
and when each is the right tool.

The position the books take is consistent: large
language models, and the coding agents built on them,
amplify analyst productivity rather than replace
analyst judgment. We argue this position by
demonstration rather than by assertion. We encourage
the reader to use the AI assistance the book
describes, to verify it the way the book describes,
and to form his or her own view.

## What this book is, in three sentences

This is a graduate practicum in the daily work of
biostatistical data analysis. It comprises eight
parts: why and with whom the work is done, the
toolkit, data in hand, documents and environments,
analysis practice, industry, analysis to audience,
and a capstone. The
test of the book, in our view, is whether, after
working through it, the reader can produce a
reproducible, defensible analysis on a real
biomedical question with an interdisciplinary team,
using AI assistance without being misled by it.
